abstract: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent–child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha.

sections.body: Alpha factors are typically weak and noisy, so discovery requires searching a large expression space while controlling spurious correlations and redundant candidates. The authors argue that many LLM-based methods keep search state mainly around provenance or trajectory, which does not show whether distant factors share subexpressions or cross-sectional exposure profiles. CosmosAlpha represents each complete evaluated factor as a node with three relation types: generation lineage, expression structure, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. Graph Flow propagates node utilities through these neighborhoods, and Pareto-guided selection preserves trade-offs among quality, fertility, and diversity. The text states that CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best overall mean rank on both CSI 300 and CSI 500.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing LLM factor miners organize search around provenance, so CosmosAlpha instead treats the evaluated factor pool as a multi-relational graph.

sections.body: The related work covers evolutionary formula search, including genetic programming systems such as AutoAlpha and AlphaEvolve, and reinforcement-learning methods such as AlphaGen and AlphaForge. It then covers LLM-driven systems, including AlphaAgent, Alpha Jungle, QuantaAlpha and AlphaAgentEvo, which retain richer workflow state. The closest structural precedents are AlphaPROBE, which uses a lineage-based directed acyclic graph, and AlphaSAGE, which encodes the syntax tree of a single expression with GFlowNets. The authors state that these methods generally do not represent the complete evaluated factor pool as a state with explicit relations among its members. Pareto archives are cited as the basis for the selection principle.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work either optimizes factor sets or keeps search history tied to one trajectory, not a shared relational pool.

sections.body:
Each evaluated factor is a node in a graph with three edge types: generation lineage, expression structure measured by Jaccard similarity over canonical subexpressions, and exposure correlation measured by the absolute daily cross-sectional Pearson correlation averaged over valid dates. Each node receives three utilities: intrinsic quality from a Quality Pareto Archive, fertility from the hypervolume gain of its best expansion outcomes, and diversity measured against a fixed high-quality reference set. Graph Flow mixes each node's utilities with those of its neighbors:

$$
F^{(k+1)}=(1-\gamma)R+\gamma PF^{(k)}
$$

Here R stacks the node utilities and P is the combined transition matrix. Parents are then drawn from successive non-dominated fronts without a fixed scalar weighting. Setting gamma to zero removes propagation and gives the ablation without graph flow.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: CosmosAlpha scores each factor on quality, fertility and diversity, propagates them through a three-relation graph, and selects parents by Pareto fronts.

sections.body: Factors are mined on the training period from April 1, 2010 to May 31, 2019, with validation used only for LightGBM early stopping and the held-out test period running from January 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025. On CSI 300, CosmosAlpha-Graph has mean rank 1.43 and leads IC, RankIC, RankICIR, ARR and IR. R&D-Agent has the best signed MDD at -24.87%, with CosmosAlpha-Graph second at -25.07%. On CSI 500 it has mean rank 1.29, while AlphaAgent leads IR and Alpha158 leads RankICIR. On CSI 300 the Graph variant exceeds CosmosAlpha-MCTS on all seven metrics. The CSI 300 ablation shows that setting gamma to zero reduces ARR from 8.44 to 5.90.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph reaches the best mean rank, 1.43 and 1.29, over seven metrics.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes CosmosAlpha as an LLM-driven framework that organizes evaluated factors as a multi-relational search state, with Graph Flow and Pareto-guided selection guiding expansion beyond local generation history. The authors report that CosmosAlpha-Graph has the best mean rank on both universes and beats the controlled MCTS variant on every reported metric. They also report that the LLM and independent-run studies show the advantage is not confined to one backbone or stochastic run. The stated limits are that the study is an offline evaluation, that backtest results are not financial advice, and that claims are limited to the evaluated universes and period. Future work will apply the method to additional markets and to high-frequency and fundamental factors.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper reports every ablation trailing the full model on all seven metrics, and the gain holds across LLM backbones and runs.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the mechanism details omitted from the method section. These include node admission rules, duplicate handling through canonical expression identity, and construction of the three relation matrices. Local neighborhoods require structure similarity of at least 0.20 and absolute correlation of at least 0.10, and each node keeps at most its Top-30 neighbors per relation. Quality is normalized against fixed anchors before hypervolume and fertility are computed. Graph Flow uses gamma equal to 0.75, each node may make fewer than five attempts, and up to four parents are selected per round. Appendix B defines the single-factor and portfolio metrics, and the appendices that follow report the three-run stability results.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers graph admission, canonical identity, relation construction, archive and fertility formulas, Graph Flow parent selection, metric definitions, and additional result tables.
